Why calculators can show different results

Same question, different assumptions

  • Your schedule matters: results use the hours and paid weeks you enter — a 2,080-hour year (40 × 52) is only the default, not your schedule.
  • Gross, not net: these tools show pay before income tax, Social Security, Medicare, and benefit deductions.
  • Rules vary: overtime eligibility, the regular rate, and state rules are not decided by the calculator — they come from your pay arrangement.
  • Averages, not checks: monthly and semi-monthly figures are annual averages (annual ÷ 12 or ÷ 24), not four weekly checks added together.

Worked example

$10,000 bonus after $180,000 of wages already earned this year, flat method, no state tax, no 401(k).

StepMathResult
1. Federal withholding22% × $10,000$2,200
2. Social Security6.2% × $4,500 still under the $184,500 wage base$279
3. Medicare1.45% × $10,000$145
4. Total withheld$2,200 + $279 + $145$2,624

Total: $7,376 take-home.

Note: Because $180,000 of wages already used most of the Social Security wage base, only $4,500 of this bonus is charged Social Security tax.

What this calculator does not do

  • Withholding is an estimate, not your final tax — the bonus is taxed at your marginal rate when you file, and the difference is refunded or owed then.
  • The aggregate method uses a standard Form W-4 with no Steps 2–4 adjustments: other income, dependents, and extra withholding are not modeled.
  • State withholding is the flat rate you enter, applied to the full bonus; some states publish their own supplemental rate, and some tax the 401(k)-reduced amount instead.
  • Local taxes, garnishments, and deductions other than the 401(k) deferral you enter are not included. Figures are for tax year 2026 only.

How is bonus tax calculated?

Federal withholding — flat method

22% of the bonus up to $1M of supplemental wages, then 37%

$5,000 × 22% = $1,100 federal withholding

FICA — Social Security & Medicare

6.2% up to the $184,500 wage base + 1.45% Medicare on the full bonus

$5,000 × 7.65% = $382.50 when wages are under the cap

Bonuses are supplemental wages in IRS Publication 15. When a bonus is paid separately from regular pay, the employer can withhold at the flat 22% rate; when it is paid together with regular pay, the employer can use the aggregate method instead. Either way, Social Security and Medicare are withheld on top, and any state rate you enter applies to the full bonus. Our guide to how bonuses are taxed walks through the same rules with a full-year example.

The 22% rule and the $1M tier

The 22% rate applies to supplemental wages up to $1,000,000 from one employer in one calendar year. Below that line the rate is optional for the employer — the flat percentage method or the aggregate method. Above $1,000,000 of supplemental wages in the year, withholding at 37% on the excess is mandatory, whichever method is used for the rest.

Example: a $1,500,000 bonus with no earlier bonuses withholds $220,000 on the first $1,000,000 (22%) plus $185,000 on the remaining $500,000 (37%) — $405,000 of federal withholding before FICA.

Bonuses already paid by the same employer earlier in the year count toward the $1,000,000. That is why the calculator asks for bonuses already paid: a $200,000 bonus after $900,000 of earlier bonuses crosses the tier, and $37,000 of it is withheld at 37%.

Flat vs aggregate: which method applies?

Flat (percentage) methodAggregate method
Bonus paid separately; 22% withheld up to $1M, 37% aboveBonus added to one regular paycheck and run through the IRS tables
The same rate at every income levelThe withholding follows your pay, frequency, and filing status
Simple to predict: bonus × 22%Can withhold more or less than 22%, depending on the combined check

With a $10,000 bonus paid on top of a $2,000 biweekly paycheck (single filer), the aggregate method withholds $2,625.93 of federal tax — more than the flat method’s $2,200 — because the combined check is annualized as if every check were that large. The take-home is $6,609.07 against $7,035.00 flat. You cannot choose the method; the employer decides for each payment, and many payroll systems always use one of the two.

How FICA applies to a bonus

Social Security is 6.2% of wages up to the 2026 wage base of $184,500 — and your regular wages reach the base first. If you have already earned $180,000 this year, only $4,500 of room remains, so a $10,000 bonus owes Social Security on $4,500 ($279.00) and Medicare on the full $10,000 ($145.00). Medicare has no cap, and an extra 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax is withheld on wages above $200,000.

Wages before the bonusBonusSocial SecurityMedicare + additional
$0$10,000$620.00$145.00
$100,000$10,000$620.00$145.00
$180,000$10,000$279.00$145.00
$190,000$20,000$0.00$380.00

The last row includes $90 of Additional Medicare Tax on the $10,000 of wages above $200,000.

What a 401(k) contribution does to a bonus

A pre-tax 401(k) deferral taken out of the bonus lowers the federal withholding base dollar for dollar — but it never lowers FICA, which is charged on the full bonus. On a $10,000 bonus, deferring $1,000 cuts flat-method federal withholding from $2,200 to $1,980, while the $765 of FICA is unchanged; $6,255 reaches your account and $1,000 goes into the plan.

Whether a bonus can carry a 401(k) election depends on the plan: some employers apply your normal deferral percentage to bonuses, others exclude bonus pay or use a separate election. See what a contribution does to a regular check with the 401(k) paycheck impact calculator.

Withholding is not the final tax

When you file, the bonus is taxed as ordinary income at your marginal rate — the same as salary. The 22% withheld is a prepayment. If your marginal rate is 12%, too much was withheld and the difference comes back in your refund; if it is 32%, you under-withheld and may owe, which a Form W-4 extra-withholding entry can fix before year-end.

The refund test: compare 22% with your marginal bracket. Below 22%, expect some of the withholding back. Above it, plan for a smaller refund or a balance due. The guide to how bonuses are taxed runs the full-year projection step by step.

Frequently asked questions

Is a bonus taxed at 40%?

There is no single 40% bonus tax rate. What leaves the check is withholding: 22% federal, 7.65% FICA, plus your state rate where one applies — which can add up to 35–40% withheld. The final tax on a bonus is your ordinary marginal rate, settled when you file.

Why is my bonus taxed so high?

Because withholding is not the final tax. Payroll applies the flat 22% federal rate (or the aggregate tables) plus Social Security and Medicare to one payment, with no standard deduction taken out first. If that overshoots your real marginal rate, the excess comes back as a refund.

Do I get bonus tax back?

You get back only the part that was over-withheld. If your marginal rate is below 22%, the flat withholding was too much and the difference returns at filing. If your marginal rate is above 22%, you may owe the difference instead.

What is the aggregate method for bonus withholding?

Your employer adds the bonus to one regular paycheck, works out withholding on the combined amount through the IRS percentage-method tables, and subtracts the withholding on the regular pay alone. The rest is withheld from the bonus. It is the employer’s choice, not yours.

Does a 401(k) contribution reduce bonus tax?

It reduces the federal withholding base, not the final tax directly and never FICA. Putting $1,000 of a $10,000 bonus into a 401(k) cuts flat-method federal withholding from $2,200 to $1,980 — $220 less withheld — while Social Security and Medicare still apply to the full $10,000.

Are bonuses taxed differently than salary?

No. A bonus is ordinary income, taxed at the same rates as salary when you file. Only the withholding during the year differs, because bonuses are supplemental wages under IRS Publication 15.

Bonus tax methodology

Visible assumptions. Checkable formulas.

The flat method withholds 22% of the bonus after any pre-tax 401(k) deferral, up to $1,000,000 of supplemental wages per employer per year, and 37% on the part above. The aggregate method annualizes regular pay plus the bonus through the IRS percentage method (2026 brackets and standard deduction, standard Form W-4) and subtracts the withholding on regular pay alone. Social Security is 6.2% of the part of the bonus under the $184,500 wage base after year-to-date wages; Medicare is 1.45% of the full bonus plus 0.9% on wages above $200,000. State withholding is the flat rate entered, applied to the full bonus. Values retain full precision until display. Read our calculation methodology.
